stem: A company runs workloads on Amazon RDS, Amazon EFS, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon EBS in many member accounts of an organization in AWS Organizations. A new regulation mandates the same backup frequency and retention period for every account. The compliance team also needs regular reports that show whether the backups comply with this policy. The company wants to centrally manage the solution across all accounts. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: mandates the same backup frequency and retention period for every account
regular reports that show whether the backups comply

options.text: Create Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policies in each member account that take snapshots on the required schedule, and export the policy settings to a shared report.
options.why: Data Lifecycle Manager automates the [creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots](../facts/backup.md#backup-faq-dlm-vs-backup-when-to-use), so the RDS, EFS and DynamoDB data gets no backups.
options.misconception: believes Data Lifecycle Manager backs up every storage and database service

options.text: Deploy an AWS Lambda function on an Amazon EventBridge schedule in each member account that backs up every resource and writes the results to a report.
options.why: It can work, but the team writes, deploys and fixes code in every account, which is far more work than one managed backup policy.

options.text: Attach an AWS Backup backup policy in AWS Organizations to the organization root, and create an AWS Backup Audit Manager framework with a report plan.
options.why: Backup policies [centrally manage and apply backup plans](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-backup-policy-effective-plan-immutable) across the accounts, and Audit Manager reports on [the compliance of your data protection policies](../facts/backup.md#backup-faq-audit-manager-purpose).

options.text: Configure the backup settings of each service in every member account, and create AWS Config rules that report on those settings each month.
options.why: Backups that a service creates itself are [not available for central governance through AWS Backup](../facts/backup.md#backup-native-service-backups-not-centrally-governed), so the work grows with every account and service.
options.misconception: believes the backup settings of each service give one central policy across accounts

explanation: The stem asks for one policy in many accounts and for proof of compliance. A backup policy in AWS Organizations applies one backup plan to the accounts, and each account receives the effective plan [as an immutable plan for that account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-backup-policy-effective-plan-immutable). AWS Backup Audit Manager creates [multi-Region and multi-account reports](../facts/backup.md#backup-faq-audit-manager-multi-account-reports) from the management account.
takeaway: One backup rule for many accounts and services: an AWS Backup policy in AWS Organizations, plus Audit Manager reports.
twin: If the stem said "only Amazon EBS volumes in one account, with no reports" instead: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, which automates EBS snapshots [at no additional cost](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-dlm-automates-snapshots-and-amis).
say: Many accounts and one backup rule: an AWS Backup policy in Organizations, and Audit Manager for the proof.

stem: A company keeps the backups of its production databases in one backup vault in AWS Backup. Auditors require that each backup stays protected for its full retention period. The backups must be immutable: no user, including the root user, can delete a backup or shorten its retention before the retention period ends. The company must ensure that this rule is enforced. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: no user, including the root user, can delete a backup

options.text: Turn on AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode for the backup vault, set a grace time, and let the grace time end without any changes.
options.why: After the grace time, a compliance-mode lock [cannot be altered or deleted by any user](../facts/backup.md#backup-vault-lock-compliance-immutable-by-anyone), and AWS Backup denies deletes [including the root user](../facts/backup.md#backup-vault-lock-denies-delete-and-lifecycle-change-even-root).

options.text: Turn on AWS Backup Vault Lock in governance mode for the backup vault, and set the minimum retention of the lock to match the backup plan.
options.why: A governance-mode vault can have its [lock removed by users with sufficient IAM permissions](../facts/backup.md#backup-vault-lock-governance-lock-removable-with-iam), so an administrator with those permissions can still delete backups.

options.text: Copy each backup to a second backup vault in another account, and turn on AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode for both backup vaults.
options.why: It works, but a second account, a second vault and a copy job for every backup add work and cost that one locked vault does not need.

options.text: Turn on the AWS Backup Audit Manager control that checks whether backup vaults prevent manual deletion of recovery points, and alert on failures.
options.why: The control [Vaults prevent manual deletion of recovery points](../facts/backup.md#backup-audit-manager-control-vault-prevent-deletion) evaluates vault settings and reports a result; it does not stop a delete.

explanation: The stem names the strongest actor, the root user. After its grace time, a compliance-mode lock [cannot be altered or deleted by any user](../facts/backup.md#backup-vault-lock-compliance-immutable-by-anyone). A governance-mode lock protects less, because users with the right IAM permissions can remove it. So one vault setting in compliance mode meets the rule, with no second vault or account.
takeaway: Even the root user is blocked: compliance mode. A security team that removes the lock: governance mode.
twin: If the stem said "members of the security team who hold a specific IAM permission must be able to remove the protection" instead: governance mode, because users [who have the appropriate IAM permissions](../facts/backup.md#backup-vault-lock-governance-lock-removable-with-iam) can remove that lock.
say: Nobody, root included, means compliance mode; a team that must remove the lock means governance mode.

stem: A company backs up the Amazon EBS volumes of its application servers with one AWS Backup plan. The plan has a daily rule and a monthly rule. The company must retain the daily backups for 30 days and the monthly backups for 7 years. The monthly backups are infrequently accessed after 30 days, and a slower restore of an old monthly backup is acceptable. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: retain the daily backups for 30 days

options.text: Add a lifecycle to the daily rule that moves each daily backup to cold storage after 1 day, and keep the monthly backups in warm storage for 7 years.
options.why: An EBS snapshot moves to cold storage when its rule runs [monthly or less often](../facts/backup.md#backup-cold-ebs-is-snapshot-archive-monthly-or-less), so the daily backups stay warm, and so do the monthly ones.

options.text: Copy the monthly backups into an Amazon S3 bucket, and add an S3 Lifecycle rule that moves the copies to S3 Glacier Deep Archive and deletes them after 7 years.
options.why: EBS snapshots sit in S3 buckets that you manage through Amazon EC2, not through the [Amazon S3 console or the Amazon S3 API](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-s3-buckets-not-accessible), so no S3 Lifecycle rule reaches them.

options.text: Keep the daily and the monthly backups in warm storage, and set the retention periods of the two rules to 30 days and 7 years.
options.why: It works, but the monthly backups stay warm for 7 years, although the lifecycle can move them to [a lower-cost cold storage tier](../facts/backup.md#backup-faq-lifecycle-warm-to-cold).
options.misconception: believes EBS backups have no cold storage tier in AWS Backup

options.text: Add a lifecycle to the monthly rule that moves each monthly backup to cold storage after 30 days and deletes it after 7 years, and keep daily backups warm.
options.why: EBS [supports a transition of backups to cold storage](../facts/backup.md#backup-ebs-supports-cold-storage-archive-tier), and the monthly rule runs [monthly or less often](../facts/backup.md#backup-cold-ebs-is-snapshot-archive-monthly-or-less), as that transition requires.

explanation: Cold storage for EBS backups is [Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive](../facts/backup.md#backup-cold-ebs-is-snapshot-archive-monthly-or-less), for rules that run monthly or less often. A backup stays in cold storage for [a minimum of 90 days](../facts/backup.md#backup-cold-storage-min-90-days-retention-rule), which the 7-year monthly backups meet and the 30-day daily backups do not. So the monthly rule gets the lifecycle, and the daily rule stays warm.
takeaway: Long, rarely read EBS backups: a lifecycle to cold storage on the monthly rule, not on the daily one.
twin: If the stem said "Amazon Aurora DB clusters" instead: keep the monthly backups in warm storage, because the [Amazon Aurora](../facts/backup.md#backup-feature-row-aurora) row has no lifecycle to cold storage.

stem: A company runs an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance for an order application and protects the DB instance with AWS Backup. A new data protection policy describes the backups that the company needs. The company must be able to restore the database to a point in time a few minutes before an error, for errors that are found within 2 weeks. The company does not want to store more backups than the policy requires. Which backup configuration is the MOST cost-effective way to meet this requirement?
keywords: restore the database to a point in time a few minutes before an error

options.text: Create a backup rule that creates a snapshot backup on the last day of every month, and set the retention period of the rule to 5 years.
options.why: [Unlike snapshot backups](../facts/backup.md#backup-continuous-rule-allows-pitr-unlike-snapshot), continuous backups allow point-in-time restore, so a monthly snapshot cannot reach a moment a few minutes before an error.
options.misconception: believes a snapshot backup allows a restore to any moment

options.text: Create a backup rule with continuous backups turned on and a retention period of 35 days, and a second rule that creates daily snapshot backups kept for 5 years.
options.why: It works, but the continuous backups are kept longer than needed, and five years of daily snapshots add storage that the policy does not ask for.

options.text: Create a backup rule with continuous backups turned on for point-in-time restore, and set the retention period of the rule to 14 days.
options.why: [Continuous backups allow you to perform point-in-time restore](../facts/backup.md#backup-continuous-rule-allows-pitr-unlike-snapshot), and a retention of two weeks covers each error that the team finds in that time.

options.text: Create a backup rule with continuous backups turned on, and add a lifecycle that moves the backups to cold storage after 35 days and deletes them after 5 years.
options.why: Cold storage needs a [minimum transition period of 90 days](../facts/backup.md#backup-pitr-no-cold-storage-because-35-vs-90), and continuous backups have a [maximum retention period of 35 days](../facts/backup.md#backup-pitr-no-cold-storage-because-35-vs-90).

explanation: A restore to a moment a few minutes before an error needs continuous backups. They rewind the database [within 1 second of precision](../facts/backup.md#backup-pitr-restore-rewinds-to-chosen-time), and their retention can range from [1 day to 35 days](../facts/backup.md#backup-retention-continuous-range). Two weeks of retention is the smallest setting that meets the policy.
takeaway: Restore to a moment a few minutes before an error: a continuous backup rule, kept as long as the policy asks.
twin: If the stem said "keep a restorable backup of the database from the end of every month for 5 years" instead: the monthly snapshot rule, because snapshot retention reaches [100 years](../facts/backup.md#backup-retention-snapshot-range).

stem: A company uses AWS Backup in the accounts of its organization in AWS Organizations. A recovery partner owns an AWS account that belongs to a different organization. If the company's accounts are compromised, the partner must be able to restore the company's backups from the partner's own account. The copies that the partner can reach must be kept in an isolated vault that is locked against deletion. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: restore the company's backups from the partner's own account

options.text: Add a copy action to the backup plan that copies each backup directly into a backup vault in the partner's AWS account.
options.why: For cross-account copies the accounts [must belong to the same organization](../facts/backup.md#backup-cross-account-requires-same-organization), and the partner's account is in another organization.

options.text: Create a logically air-gapped vault in AWS Backup, and add a copy action to the backup plan that copies each backup into this vault.
options.why: In a logically air-gapped vault, [immutable backups are locked by default](../facts/backup.md#backup-faq-lag-vault-locked-by-default), and a copy action fills the vault with no code to maintain.

options.text: Share the standard backup vault that holds the backups with the partner's AWS account by using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).
options.why: A standard backup vault is [Not compatible with AWS RAM](../facts/backup.md#backup-lag-vs-standard-sharing-row), and its access is managed through policies and AWS Organizations.
options.misconception: believes a standard backup vault can be shared through AWS RAM

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function that starts a copy job for each new backup every day and copies the backup into a logically air-gapped vault.
options.why: It works, but the company writes and runs code for each copy job, although a copy action in the backup plan does the same work.

options.text: Share the logically air-gapped vault with the partner's AWS account ID by using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).
options.why: AWS RAM shares the vault [with accounts in different Organizations](../facts/backup.md#backup-faq-lag-vault-share-ram), and its backups can be [restored from a different account](../facts/backup.md#backup-faq-lag-vault-ransomware-strategy).

explanation: The partner is outside the organization, so a direct cross-account copy fails. A logically air-gapped vault keeps the copies locked, and it can be shared [through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM)](../facts/backup.md#backup-faq-lag-vault-share-ram). The partner then restores from its own account.
takeaway: Backups for an account outside the organization: copy them to a logically air-gapped vault and share it through AWS RAM.
twin: If the stem said "a recovery account in the same organization" instead: a copy action into that account works, because the accounts [must belong to the same organization](../facts/backup.md#backup-cross-account-requires-same-organization).

stem: A company keeps the backups of its production databases in one backup vault in AWS Backup. Auditors require that each backup stays protected for its full retention period. Most users must not be able to delete a backup or shorten its retention, but members of the security team who hold a specific IAM permission must be able to remove the protection. The company must ensure that this rule is enforced. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: members of the security team who hold a specific IAM permission must be able to remove the protection

options.text: Turn on AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode for the backup vault, set a grace time, and let the grace time end without any changes.
options.why: After the grace time, a compliance-mode lock [cannot be altered or deleted by any user](../facts/backup.md#backup-vault-lock-compliance-immutable-by-anyone), so the security team loses the ability to remove it.
options.misconception: believes the strictest lock fits every requirement, also one that needs a removable lock

options.text: Turn on AWS Backup Vault Lock in governance mode for the backup vault, and set the minimum retention of the lock to match the backup plan.
options.why: In governance mode, [only designated personnel can make changes](../facts/backup.md#backup-vault-lock-governance-intent-designated-personnel): users [who have the appropriate IAM permissions](../facts/backup.md#backup-vault-lock-governance-lock-removable-with-iam) can remove the lock.

options.text: Copy each backup to a second backup vault in another account, and turn on AWS Backup Vault Lock in governance mode for both backup vaults.
options.why: It works, but a second account, a second vault and a copy job for every backup add work and cost that one locked vault does not need.

options.text: Turn on the AWS Backup Audit Manager control that checks whether backup vaults prevent manual deletion of recovery points, and alert on failures.
options.why: The control [Vaults prevent manual deletion of recovery points](../facts/backup.md#backup-audit-manager-control-vault-prevent-deletion) evaluates vault settings and reports a result; it does not stop a delete.

explanation: The stem asks for protection that one named team can remove. A governance-mode vault can have its [lock removed by users with sufficient IAM permissions](../facts/backup.md#backup-vault-lock-governance-lock-removable-with-iam), so other users keep the protection and the security team can still remove it.
takeaway: A lock that a security team with an IAM permission can remove: Vault Lock in governance mode.
twin: If the stem said "no user, including the root user, can delete a backup or shorten its retention" instead: compliance mode, because after the grace time it [cannot be altered or deleted by any user](../facts/backup.md#backup-vault-lock-compliance-immutable-by-anyone).

stem: A company backs up an unencrypted Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with AWS Backup. The backups are stored in a backup vault that uses an AWS managed key. A new security policy mandates that every backup of the database is encrypted at rest with a customer managed AWS KMS key. The database must keep its current engine and data, and a short maintenance window is acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: unencrypted Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance
encrypted at rest with a customer managed AWS KMS key

options.text: Create a new backup vault that uses the customer managed key, and change the backup plan so that it stores the backups of the DB instance in the new vault.
options.why: The vault key [applies to the backups of certain resource types](../facts/backup.md#backup-vault-key-applies-only-to-independent-encryption-types), and RDS snapshots keep the key used to [encrypt the source Amazon RDS database](../facts/backup.md#backup-encryption-rds-row).

options.text: Modify the DB instance to turn on encryption at rest with the customer managed key, and keep the current backup plan and the current backup vault.
options.why: You can [only encrypt an Amazon RDS DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-only-at-create) when you create it, so a modification cannot turn on encryption for this instance.

options.text: Create a new encrypted DB instance, copy the data into it with an AWS Database Migration Service task, and back up the new DB instance with the plan.
options.why: It works, but a migration task, a new empty database and a full data copy are more work than a snapshot copy and a restore.

options.text: Take a snapshot, copy it with encryption under the customer managed key, restore a new DB instance from the encrypted copy, and back up the new DB instance.
options.why: You can [encrypt a copy of an unencrypted snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-encrypt-existing-via-snapshot-copy) and [restore an encrypted DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-encrypt-existing-via-snapshot-copy) from it, and AWS Backup then backs up an encrypted database.

explanation: AWS Backup does not encrypt RDS backups with the vault key: RDS snapshots use the key that is used to [encrypt the source Amazon RDS database](../facts/backup.md#backup-encryption-rds-row). So the company encrypts the database itself. The shortest path is to [encrypt a copy of an unencrypted snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-encrypt-existing-via-snapshot-copy) and restore a new DB instance from that copy.
takeaway: RDS backups keep the key of the database: encrypt the database through a snapshot copy, not through the vault key.
twin: If the stem said "an unencrypted Amazon EFS file system" instead: the new backup vault works, because [Amazon EFS backups are always encrypted](../facts/backup.md#backup-encryption-efs-row) with the key of the backup vault.

stem: A company runs an internal reporting application on Amazon EC2 instances with an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database in one AWS Region. The company needs cross-Region disaster recovery for the application. If the Region fails, it is acceptable to restore service within one day and to lose up to one day of data. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: acceptable to restore service within one day
lose up to one day of data

options.text: Create a cross-Region read replica of the database and a stopped copy of the application in a second Region, and promote the replica after a Region failure.
options.why: It works, but in pilot light [your core infrastructure is always available](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-cmp-wp-pilot-light-core-infrastructure-always-available), so the replica runs and costs money every day.

options.text: Back up the instances and the database daily with AWS Backup, copy each backup to a backup vault in a second Region, and restore there after a Region failure.
options.why: A backup plan can copy [in the same or another AWS Region](../facts/backup.md#backup-copy-action-same-or-other-region-and-account), and daily copies keep the data loss within the one day that the stem accepts.

options.text: Run a scaled-down copy of the application and a cross-Region read replica of the database in a second Region, and scale out after a Region failure.
options.why: A warm standby [decreases the time to recovery](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-cmp-wp-warm-standby-faster-than-pilot-light), but the stem accepts one day, and the copy of the application runs and costs money every day.

options.text: Convert the database to a Multi-AZ deployment, and run the EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones of the Region.
options.why: For Multi-AZ, the [Main purpose is high availability](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-purpose-ha-dr-scale) inside one Region, so the failure of the Region still stops the application.

explanation: The stem sets an [RPO](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-rpo-definition) and an [RTO](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-rto-definition) of one day each. Backups copied to a second Region meet both, and nothing runs in that Region until a disaster. Pilot light and warm standby keep resources running in the second Region every day, which costs more than the stem needs.
takeaway: Data loss and recovery time of a day are acceptable: back up, copy to a second Region, and restore after a disaster.
twin: If the stem said "recover within minutes after a Region failure" instead: a warm standby, because a copy that runs all the time [decreases the time to recovery](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-cmp-wp-warm-standby-faster-than-pilot-light).

stem: A company runs an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance for an order application and protects the DB instance with AWS Backup. A new data protection policy describes the backups that the company needs. The company must keep a restorable backup of the database from the end of every month for 5 years. The company does not want to store more backups than the policy requires. Which backup configuration is the MOST cost-effective way to meet this requirement?
keywords: keep a restorable backup of the database from the end of every month for 5 years

options.text: Create a backup rule that creates a snapshot backup on the last day of every month, and set the retention period of the rule to 5 years.
options.why: A monthly snapshot rule fits the schedule, and snapshot retention can range [between 1 day and 100 years](../facts/backup.md#backup-retention-snapshot-range), so 5 years is a valid setting.

options.text: Create a backup rule with continuous backups turned on and a retention period of 35 days, and a second rule that creates daily snapshot backups kept for 5 years.
options.why: It works, but the continuous backups and the daily snapshots store far more backups than the monthly policy asks for.

options.text: Create a backup rule with continuous backups turned on for point-in-time restore, and set the retention period of the rule to 14 days.
options.why: Continuous backups keep a retention of [1 day to 35 days](../facts/backup.md#backup-retention-continuous-range), so they cannot hold a backup from the end of every month for 5 years.
options.misconception: believes continuous backups also cover long-term retention

options.text: Create a backup rule with continuous backups turned on, and add a lifecycle that moves the backups to cold storage after 35 days and deletes them after 5 years.
options.why: Cold storage needs a [minimum transition period of 90 days](../facts/backup.md#backup-pitr-no-cold-storage-because-35-vs-90), and continuous backups have a [maximum retention period of 35 days](../facts/backup.md#backup-pitr-no-cold-storage-because-35-vs-90).

explanation: The stem asks for one backup per month, kept for 5 years. Snapshot backups can be stored for [a maximum of 100 years](../facts/backup.md#backup-snapshot-hourly-and-100-years), and continuous backups stop at [35 days](../facts/backup.md#backup-retention-continuous-range). A monthly snapshot rule with a retention of 5 years stores the fewest backups that meet the policy.
takeaway: Keep backups for years: a snapshot backup rule. Restore to a recent moment: a continuous backup rule.
twin: If the stem said "restore the database to a point in time a few minutes before an error, for errors that are found within 2 weeks" instead: the continuous rule, because [continuous backups allow you to perform point-in-time restore](../facts/backup.md#backup-continuous-rule-allows-pitr-unlike-snapshot).

stem: A company stores customer orders in an Amazon DynamoDB global table with replicas in two AWS Regions. The order data must be durable. The company has no backups of the table. Last week, a faulty deployment overwrote the status attribute of many items, and the change appeared in both Regions. The company must be able to return the table to a point in time before a faulty change in the future. What should the company do?
keywords: the change appeared in both Regions
return the table to a point in time before a faulty change

options.text: Fail over the application to the replica in the second Region when a faulty change is found.
options.why: DynamoDB [automatically replicates the write to all other replicas](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-global-table-write-replicated-automatically), so the second Region holds the same overwritten items.

options.text: Add a replica of the global table in a third Region to keep one more copy of the items.
options.why: A third replica receives the same writes, because DynamoDB [automatically replicates the write to all other replicas](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-global-table-write-replicated-automatically), so it copies the faulty change too.

options.text: Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table so that the table can be restored to a chosen second.
options.why: Point-in-time recovery protects tables [from accidental write or delete operations](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-pitr-protects-accidental-writes-deletes), so the company can restore the table to a moment before a faulty change.

options.text: Turn on DynamoDB Streams for the table so that the stream keeps a record of every change to the items.
options.why: Stream records have a [lifetime of 24 hours](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-stream-records-24-hours), and a stream does not restore a table to an earlier state.

explanation: A replica follows every change, so a replica is not a backup. A recovery point keeps [the content of a resource at a specified time](../facts/backup.md#backup-faq-recovery-point-definition), and point-in-time recovery creates such points for the table. After a faulty change, the company restores the table to a second before the change.
takeaway: A replica copies mistakes too. To undo a bad write, restore from point-in-time recovery or a backup.
twin: If the stem said "keep monthly backups of the table for 7 years" instead: AWS Backup snapshot backups, because their retention can range [between 1 day and 100 years](../facts/backup.md#backup-retention-snapshot-range).
say: A replica copies the mistake to every Region. Point-in-time recovery takes you back to before it.

stem: A company uses AWS Backup to protect Amazon RDS databases and Amazon EFS file systems. For an external audit, the company must show every month that its backups can be restored and that each restore finishes within a target restore time. The company wants to produce this evidence with the LEAST operational overhead. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
keywords: each restore finishes within a target restore time

options.text: Create a restore testing plan in AWS Backup that restores selected recovery points of the databases and the file systems on a monthly schedule.
options.why: Restore testing gives [automated and periodic evaluation of restore viability](../facts/backup.md#backup-restore-testing-automated-periodic-evaluation), and the plan sets [the frequency for your restore tests](../facts/backup.md#backup-restore-testing-plan-steps).

options.text: Assign an engineer to restore one backup by hand each month, measure the restore time, and record the results in a shared spreadsheet.
options.why: It works, but an engineer repeats the restore and the record keeping by hand every month, although restore testing runs on a schedule.

options.text: Create an AWS CloudTrail trail that records the AWS Backup API calls, and give the auditors read access to the logged backup job events.
options.why: CloudTrail gives a [consolidated view of backup activity logs](../facts/backup.md#backup-faq-cloudtrail-activity-logs), which shows the API calls, not whether a restore works in time.

options.text: Create an AWS Backup Audit Manager framework with the control that checks restore time against a target, and add a report plan for the framework.
options.why: The control [Restore time for resources meet target](../facts/backup.md#backup-audit-manager-control-restore-time) checks the restore testing jobs, and Audit Manager [automatically generates a new report for you every 24 hours](../facts/backup.md#backup-audit-manager-frameworks-and-daily-reports).

options.text: Turn on AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode for the backup vaults that hold the recovery points of the databases and the file systems.
options.why: Vault Lock helps [prevent manual deletion of backups](../facts/backup.md#backup-faq-vault-lock-purpose-worm), but a lock does not test whether a backup can be restored.
options.misconception: believes a locked backup is proof that the backup can be restored

explanation: The audit needs two proofs: restores work, and they finish in time. A restore testing plan runs restores on a schedule and can [monitor restore job duration times](../facts/backup.md#backup-restore-testing-automated-periodic-evaluation). An Audit Manager framework compares each test with the target and reports the result, so no engineer restores by hand.
takeaway: Proof that restores work and finish in time: restore testing plus an Audit Manager restore time control.
twin: If the stem said "show that every backup is encrypted" instead: the Audit Manager control [Recovery points are encrypted](../facts/backup.md#backup-audit-manager-control-encrypted), without restore tests.
say: Restore testing runs the restores for you, and Audit Manager reports whether they met the target time.

stem: A company protects an Amazon EFS file system with AWS Backup. A faulty script changed many files in the file system. An administrator ran a full restore of last night's recovery point into the existing file system, and the restore job completed. However, the application currently reads the changed files from their original paths. The company must ensure that the application reads the restored files. Which next step will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: full restore of last night's recovery point into the existing file system
reads the changed files from their original paths

options.text: Run the restore job again with the setting that overwrites the existing files at their original paths in the file system.
options.why: AWS Backup [does not support destructive restores with Amazon EFS](../facts/backup.md#backup-restore-efs-no-destructive-restore-recovery-directory), so no restore setting overwrites the files at their original paths.

options.text: Move or copy the restored files from the recovery directory under the root of the file system back to their original paths.
options.why: After a full restore, the files are [located in a recovery subdirectory under the root](../facts/backup.md#backup-restore-efs-files-not-in-original-locations), so a move or a copy puts them where the application reads.

options.text: Restore the same recovery point to a new EFS file system, and mount the new file system on the application instances in place of the old one.
options.why: It adds a second file system, and the files still land in a recovery subdirectory, because [Files are not restored to their original locations](../facts/backup.md#backup-restore-efs-files-not-in-original-locations).
options.misconception: believes a full restore to a new file system places the files at their original paths

options.text: Write a script that compares each restored file with the file at its original path and copies every restored file that differs over the changed file.
options.why: It works, but writing and testing a comparison script is more work than moving the restored files back to their original paths.

explanation: An EFS restore does not overwrite files. AWS Backup restores the file system to a [recovery directory off of the root directory](../facts/backup.md#backup-restore-efs-no-destructive-restore-recovery-directory), and [Files are not restored to their original locations](../facts/backup.md#backup-restore-efs-files-not-in-original-locations). The restore worked; the last step is to move the files back.
takeaway: An EFS restore lands in a recovery directory under the root: move the files back yourself.
twin: If the stem said "an Amazon RDS DB instance" instead: point the application to the restored DB instance, because AWS Backup [creates a new resource during restore](../facts/backup.md#backup-restore-destructive-exceptions-listed).

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the next step that makes the application read the restored files, with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: a full EFS restore into the existing file system completed, and the application still reads the changed files at their original paths.
Before I look at the options, I predict that the restored files are in another place, because an EFS restore does not overwrite files: AWS Backup puts them in a recovery directory under the root.

I remove the option that runs the restore again with an overwrite setting, because EFS has no destructive restore. I remove the restore to a new file system, because a full restore puts the files in a recovery subdirectory there too.
Between moving the files back and writing a comparison script, the difference is the work; the stem asks for the least overhead, so I choose the move or copy from the recovery directory.
Check: moving the files back meets every constraint and needs no new resource. Time: 90 seconds.
